source_title: Forest Research Institute develops technique to produce up to 30 neem plants from one in a yr - The Times of India
source_excerpt: Dehradun: Forest Research Institute (FRI) in Dehradun has developed a propagation technique that can produce up to 30 new neem plants from a single plant in a year, a development that researchers say could boost neem cultivation and support organic farming.The technique combines tissue culture with mini-cutting methods and has recorded a success rate of 95-100%, scientist âGâ in FRIâs genetics division, Ajay Thakur, said.âNeem has applications in agriculture and industry and its oil contains compounds such as azadirachtin and nimbin, which help repel around 700 insect species. The plant is used in organic farming, neem-coated urea, and medicinal and personal-care products. The technique can help increase the availability of quality neem plants to meet this demand,â Thakur said, adding that despite neem being native to India, the country continues to import neem-based raw material.Launched in 2016 in collaboration with the Indian Farmers Fertiliser Cooperative (IFFCO) following the govtâs push for neem-coated urea in 2015, the research programme has received funding of over Rs 5 crore and has been extended for another five years, officials said.FRI initially identified high-yielding neem varieties that could begin bearing fruit in their second year, compared with the usual wait of around six years. âWe focused on cloning these varieties to retain their desirable traits instead of using seeds. The hybrid method uses micropropagation through tissue culture and a mini-cutting technique,â Thakur said.He added that cuttings were planted during the monsoon, usually in July, and allowed to grow for six to seven months until they reached a height of around one metre.âThey are then transferred to the ground during winter, preferably to protected areas where irrigation and fertilisation could be managed, or kept in grow bags. In Jan, the plants are cut back to around 45-50cm from the base, which encourages new shoots to emerge approximately every two months, though the timing varies depending on climatic conditions,â he said.Small pieces of stem, each containing a bud, are then cut from the plant, treated with fungicide and dipped in rooting hormone. The cuttings are then planted in vermiculite, a soilless growing medium that provides physical support but does not supply nutrients. Rooting in this begins within 21 days to a month, Thakur said.âFRI currently gets an average of four to five harvests from a plant in the first year.
